Let $S$ be any set, possibly infinite, and let $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be a Coxeter matrix: $m(s,s)=1$, and for distinct $s,t$, $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$. Let $F(S)$ be the free group on $S$, let $N$ be the normal closure of
$$
\{s^2:s\in S\}\cup\{(st)^{m(s,t)}:s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty\},
$$
and define $W=F(S)/N$. The image of $s\in S$ in $W$ is also denoted $s$. This is the Coxeter group presented by $(S,m)$.

For $w\in W$, define its length by
$$
\ell(w)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N: w=s_1\cdots s_k\text{ for some }s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\}.
$$
The set is nonempty because every element of the quotient has a finite word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ and the relators give $s^{-1}=s$; its minimum exists by the well-ordering principle. A word of length $\ell(w)$ for $w$ is a reduced expression; the empty word is the reduced expression of $1$.

Define the reflection set $T=\{x s x^{-1}:x\in W,\ s\in S\}$. Write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for a reflection $t\in T$ and $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. Define the reflection-chain Bruhat order by $u\le v$ if there is a finite chain $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain is allowed. Length strictly increases on each nonempty chain, so this relation is a partial order. The exact reduced-subword description and finite-interval consequence needed below are established in [[thm-arbitrary-rank-finite-parabolics-and-bruhat-subword]].

When $S$ is finite, the presentation and length agree with [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and the reflection-chain order agrees with [[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]. No exchange, standard-parabolic, reduced-subword, or interval-finiteness property is included in this definition; those properties are justified separately.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group, $\ell$ its length function, and let $T$, $\eta$, $\Phi$ and the right action of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ be as in [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]].

1. **Sign character and parity.** There is a unique homomorphism $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ for all $s\in S$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ for all $w\in W$. Consequently, for all $w\in W$ and $s\in S$,
$$\ell(sw)=\ell(w)\pm1,\qquad \ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1,$$
with $\ell(sw)\equiv\ell(w)+1\pmod2$ and $\ell(ws)\equiv\ell(w)+1\pmod2$.
2. **Exchange.** Let $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ be a reduced expression and let $s\in S$ satisfy $\ell(sw)=k-1$. Then
$$sw=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_k$$
for some $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$; equivalently, $w$ has a reduced expression beginning with $s$, and $s$ is a prefix reflection of any reduced expression of $w$. Right-handed form: if $\ell(ws)=k-1$ then $ws=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_k$ for some $i$.
3. **Deletion.** If the word $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ in $S$ is not reduced, then there are $i<j$ with
$$s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots\widehat{s_j}\cdots s_k=s_1\cdots s_k .$$
Hence repeated deletion of two letters transforms every word into a reduced expression for the same element, and a word is reduced if and only if it cannot be shortened by deleting two letters.
4. **Faithfulness of the signed action.** The right action of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ is faithful, so $W$ embeds in $\operatorname{Sym}(\{\pm1\}\times T)$; in particular distinct simple generators are distinct in $W$.

Let $(S,m)$ be a Coxeter matrix ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), let $W$ be the presented group with length function $\ell$ and identity $1$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), and let
$$T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$$
be its set of reflections ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]] (2)).

**(1) The Bruhat graph and the Bruhat order.** For $u,v\in W$ write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for some $t\in T$ with $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. The directed graph on $W$ with these edges is the **Bruhat graph** of $(W,S)$. Define $u\le v$ if there exist $u_0,\dots,u_k\in W$ with $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain ($k=0$) is allowed, so $u\le u$ for every $u$. This relation is the **Bruhat order** on $W$. Both $\to$ and $\le$ are predicates on $W\times W$ defined from the length function of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and chains in the definition of $\le$ are finite sequences of elements of $W$, so both relations are well defined; every object below is a subset or a predicate on the fixed group $W$, and no choice principle is used anywhere in this definition.

**(2) Partial order and the identity.** $\le$ is a partial order on $W$: it is reflexive and transitive by construction (an empty chain, and concatenation of chains), and it is antisymmetric because $\ell$ strictly increases along every edge, so a chain from $u$ to $v$ containing at least one edge satisfies $\ell(u)<\ell(v)$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). Consequently $u\le v$ together with $\ell(u)=\ell(v)$ forces $u=v$, and every $u<v$ (that is, $u\le v$ and $u\ne v$) satisfies $\ell(u)<\ell(v)$. Moreover $1\le w$ for every $w\in W$: for a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$ one has $\ell(w_j)=j$ (a shorter expression for the prefix $s_1\cdots s_j$, substituted into $s_1\cdots s_k$, would be a word of length $<k$ for $w$), so $w_{j-1}\to w_j$ because $w_{j-1}^{-1}w_j=s_j=1\cdot s_j\cdot 1^{-1}\in T$ and $\ell(w_j)=j>\ell(w_{j-1})=j-1$ ([[def-group]]).

**(3) Inversion and left multiplication.** For all $u,v\in W$ one has $u\le v$ if and only if $u^{-1}\le v^{-1}$. More precisely, a chain $u=u_0\to\cdots\to u_k=v$ with $u_{j+1}=u_jt_j$, $t_j\in T$, inverts to the chain $u^{-1}=u_0^{-1}\to\cdots\to u_k^{-1}=v^{-1}$, because
$$u_{j+1}^{-1}=t_ju_j^{-1}=u_j^{-1}\,(u_jt_ju_j^{-1})$$
with $u_jt_ju_j^{-1}\in T$ and $\ell(u_{j+1}^{-1})=\ell(u_{j+1})>\ell(u_j)=\ell(u_j^{-1})$; here $\ell(x)=\ell(x^{-1})$ holds because reversing a reduced expression of $x$ gives a reduced expression of $x^{-1}$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3)). Consequently the order is also generated by left multiplication by reflections: if $x\in W$, $t\in T$ and $\ell(tx)>\ell(x)$, then $x\to tx$, since $x^{-1}(tx)=x^{-1}tx\in T$ and $T$ is closed under conjugation ([[def-group]]).

**(4) Reflection parity.** If $x\in W$ and $t\in T$ then $\ell(xt)\equiv\ell(x)+1\pmod 2$, so $\ell(xt)\ne\ell(x)$; in particular $x\to xt$ if and only if $\ell(xt)>\ell(x)$, and for each pair $(x,t)$ exactly one of the relations $x\to xt$, $xt\to x$ holds. Indeed [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]] (1) supplies the sign character $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ for all $s\in S$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(x)=(-1)^{\ell(x)}$ for all $x\in W$; as $\operatorname{sgn}$ is a homomorphism into the abelian group $\{\pm1\}$ ([[def-group]]) one has $\operatorname{sgn}(wsw^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ for every $w\in W$ and $s\in S$, so $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=-1$ for every $t\in T$, and then $\operatorname{sgn}(xt)=-\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ gives the asserted congruence.

The **interval** $[u,v]:=\{x\in W:u\le x\le v\}$ and the statement that $\ell$ is a rank function are introduced only after the saturated-chain results of [[lem-cg-bruhat-chain-refinement-and-gradedness]]. The subword description of $\le$ used throughout this page is the theorem [[thm-cg-bruhat-subword-characterization]], the recorded justifier of this definition; no subword assertion is made here.

Let $w\in W$ have reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_q$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]) and let $\le$ be the Bruhat order ([[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]).

**(1) Subword criterion.** For every $u\in W$,
$$u\le w\iff\text{there exist }1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le q\text{ with }u=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k},$$
and the indices may be chosen with $k=\ell(u)$, so that $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ is then a reduced expression of $u$.

**(2) Expression independence.** For all $u,w\in W$ the following are equivalent: (a) $u\le w$; (b) every reduced expression of $w$ has a subword that is a reduced expression of $u$; (c) some reduced expression of $w$ has a subword that is a reduced expression of $u$.

**(3) The identity.** In particular $1\le w$ for every $w\in W$: the empty subword of any reduced expression realizes the identity.

derivations.claim: **Finite-generator parabolic embedding.** The image of $\phi_J$ is $\langle J\rangle$, since its image is generated by the named generators. To prove injectivity, let $g\in W_J^*$ map to $1$, and represent $g$ by a word $u$ in $J$. In the free group $F(S)$, the word $u$ lies in the normal closure of the Coxeter relators by [F1]. By the definition of a generated normal subgroup, $u$ is a finite product of conjugates of relators and their inverses. Let $K$ contain $J$ and every letter appearing in these finitely many conjugating words and relators. The same finite product identity holds in $F(K)$, so $u$ is the identity in the Coxeter group presented on $K$. Applying [F2] to the finite system on $K$ and its subset $J$ shows that the map from $W_J^*$ into this group is injective. Hence $g=1$.

**Intrinsic and ambient lengths.** Every $J$-word is an $S$-word, so ambient length is at most intrinsic $J$-length. Conversely, take $w\in W_J^*$ and a reduced ambient expression for $\phi_J(w)$, of length $r$. Let $K$ contain $J$ and the letters in that expression. By step 1.1 applied to $K$, the presentation on $K$ embeds in $W$; thus the equality between a $J$-word for $w$ and the chosen ambient word already holds in the group on $K$. By [F2], intrinsic $J$-length equals $K$-length on $W_J^*$. The chosen expression gives $K$-length at most $r$, while every $K$-word is also an $S$-word and so has length at least $r$. Hence both lengths equal $r$, proving intrinsic and ambient length equality.

**Simple-generator length changes.** Fix $s\in S$ and $w\in W$. Choose a finite $K$ containing $s$ and the letters of a word for $w$. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 embed the group on $K$ and preserve lengths. Applying [F3] in that finite-generator system gives both asserted $\pm1$ formulas in $W$.

**Bruhat comparison implies a subword.** Suppose $y\le w$, and fix a reduced expression of $w$. Choose a finite Bruhat chain from $y$ to $w$. Each element in this chain has finite word support, and each reflection used in an edge is a conjugate of a simple generator by a finite word. The union of these supports and the letters of the fixed expression of $w$ is contained in a finite $K\subseteq S$. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, the chain lies in the embedded finite-generator group on $K$ with all lengths preserved; its edges are still right multiplications by reflections. The finite-generator subword theorem [F5] now gives a reduced expression of $y$ as a subword of the fixed expression of $w$.

**A reduced subword implies Bruhat comparison.** Suppose a reduced expression of $y$ occurs as a subword of a fixed reduced expression of $w$. Let $J$ be the finite support of that expression of $w$. The subword theorem [F5] gives $y\le w$ in the finite-generator Coxeter group on $J$. By steps 1.1 and 2.1 its presentation embeds in $W$ and preserves lengths; each reflection in the finite Bruhat chain maps to a reflection in $W$. The chain therefore gives $y\le w$ in the global reflection-chain order.

Every element below $w$ is represented by a subword of a fixed reduced expression of $w$, by step 3.2. There are at most $2^{\ell(w)}$ such subwords, so the lower interval is finite with the stated bound. A strict comparison has a nonempty length-increasing chain by [F1], hence $\ell(y)<\ell(w)$ when $y<w$. Steps 3.1–3.3 prove all remaining clauses. All supports, products in the normal closure, and chains used above are finite.

boundaries.evidence: For J empty the presented subgroup is trivial; the empty reduced word and length-zero chain are included in steps 1.1 and 3.2–3.3.

Step 3.1 transfers the ±1 simple-generator length law, including length-one elements.

thm-arbitrary-rank-finite-parabolics-and.finite_check_disposition: All finite coefficient, matrix-unit, cell-filtration and example calculations are proved symbolically in the numbered proof. No executable finite-smoke assertion is claimed.

Let $S$ be any set, possibly infinite, and let $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be a Coxeter matrix: $m(s,s)=1$, and for distinct $s,t$, $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$. Let $F(S)$ be the free group on $S$, let $N$ be the normal closure of
$$
\{s^2:s\in S\}\cup\{(st)^{m(s,t)}:s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty\},
$$
and define $W=F(S)/N$. The image of $s\in S$ in $W$ is also denoted $s$. This is the Coxeter group presented by $(S,m)$.

For $w\in W$, define its length by
$$
\ell(w)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N: w=s_1\cdots s_k\text{ for some }s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\}.
$$
The set is nonempty because every element of the quotient has a finite word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ and the relators give $s^{-1}=s$; its minimum exists by the well-ordering principle. A word of length $\ell(w)$ for $w$ is a reduced expression; the empty word is the reduced expression of $1$.

Define the reflection set $T=\{x s x^{-1}:x\in W,\ s\in S\}$. Write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for a reflection $t\in T$ and $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. Define the reflection-chain Bruhat order by $u\le v$ if there is a finite chain $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain is allowed. Length strictly increases on each nonempty chain, so this relation is a partial order. The exact reduced-subword description and finite-interval consequence needed below are established in [[thm-arbitrary-rank-finite-parabolics-and-bruhat-subword]].

When $S$ is finite, the presentation and length agree with [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and the reflection-chain order agrees with [[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]. No exchange, standard-parabolic, reduced-subword, or interval-finiteness property is included in this definition; those properties are justified separately.

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter matrix $m$, and let $W,\ell,T,\le$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. For a finite $J\subseteq S$, let $W_J^*$ be the group presented by the restricted matrix $m|_J$, and let $\phi_J:W_J^*\to W$ send each generator to the same-named element.

1. The map $\phi_J$ is injective with image $\langle J\rangle$, and intrinsic length in $W_J^*$ equals ambient length in $W$ on this subgroup.
2. For $y,w\in W$, $y\le w$ if and only if a reduced expression of $y$ occurs as a subword of any fixed reduced expression of $w$. In particular, the interval $\{y:y\le w\}$ is finite and has at most $2^{\ell(w)}$ elements.
3. For every $s\in S$ and $w\in W$, $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)\pm1$ and $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix; let $W$ and $\ell$ be the presented group and its length and let $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ be the geometric representation, as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], with reflection set $T$ and sign-change sets $\Phi(w)$ as in that lemma. Parts (1) and (2) hold for every finite $S$, including the empty and singleton cases; a distinct pair is required only for part (3).

1. **Braid moves.** Call two words in $S$ *braid-equivalent* when one is obtained from the other by finitely many replacements of an alternating subword $s\,t\,s\,t\cdots$ of length $m(s,t)<\infty$ by the alternating word $t\,s\,t\,s\cdots$ of the same length. Then any two reduced expressions of the same element $w\in W$ are braid-equivalent.
2. **M-reducedness.** A word is reduced if and only if no sequence of braid moves followed by cancellation of a consecutive equal pair can shorten it (M-reduced in the sense of [Davis, Definition 3.4.1]).
3. **Singleton detection in dihedral subgroups.** Fix distinct $s,t\in S$ and put $m:=m(s,t)$. The subgroup $\langle s,t\rangle\le W$ is dihedral of order $2m$ when $m<\infty$ and infinite dihedral when $m=\infty$; every element of $\langle s,t\rangle$ acts on the quotient $E/\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$ as the identity, while for every $u\in S\setminus\{s,t\}$ one has $\sigma_u(\alpha_u)-\alpha_u=-2\alpha_u\notin\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$ (no induced quotient map for $\sigma_u$ is assumed). Consequently
$$S\cap\langle s,t\rangle=\{s,t\},$$
and every element of $\langle s,t\rangle$ has a reduced expression with all letters in $\{s,t\}$ (so the alternating words of length $q\le m$, and any $q$ when $m=\infty$, are reduced in $W$).

Let $(W,S)$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. A **totally ordered abelian group** $(\Gamma,+,0,<)$ is an abelian group with a total order invariant under translation. Its group algebra $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ consists of finite sums $\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}a_\gamma v^\gamma$, where $a_\gamma\in\mathbb Z$, with $v^\gamma v^\delta=v^{\gamma+\delta}$. Define the ring involution $\overline{v^\gamma}=v^{-\gamma}$, and set
$$
A_{<0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma<0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma,\qquad A_{\le0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma\le0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma.
$$

A **weight function** is a map $L:W\to\Gamma$ such that $L(xy)=L(x)+L(y)$ whenever $\ell(xy)=\ell(x)+\ell(y)$. Its simple-generator parameters are $L(s)$ for $s\in S$. The exact criterion for prescribing those values on the simple generators is proved in [[lem-simple-generator-weights-extend-to-a-weight-function]]. No sign restriction on $L(s)$ is part of this definition.

The coefficient ordering used on the weighted Kazhdan–Lusztig basis is the given order on $\Gamma$, through $A_{<0}$. The group algebra elements $v^{L(s)}$ are units for every $s\in S$.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, and let $K$, $E$, $(\alpha_s)_{s\in S}$, the constants $c_{st}$ and the linear maps $\sigma_s$ be as in [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]]; let $W$ and $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The involution, representation, signed-action and word assertions below hold for every finite $S$, including $S=\varnothing$ and $\#S=1$. Only the rank-two assertions require distinct generators.

1. **Involutions.** $\sigma_s^2=\mathrm{id}_E$ for every $s\in S$; each $\sigma_s$ is invertible, and $\ell(s)=1$.
2. **The rank-two block.** For any distinct $s,t\in S$, put $m:=m(s,t)$, $c:=c_{st}$, $P:=\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)\subseteq E$, $A:=\sigma_s\sigma_t$ and $B:=A|_P$. Then $A(P)\subseteq P$, and in the basis $(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$,
$$B(\alpha_s)=(c^2-1)\alpha_s+c\,\alpha_t,\qquad B(\alpha_t)=-c\,\alpha_s-\alpha_t;\qquad \operatorname{tr}(B)=c^2-2,\qquad \det(B)=1 .$$
Moreover $A(v)-v\in P$ for every $v\in E$. Consequently $E=P\oplus Q$ with $Q:=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_u:u\in S,\ u\notin\{s,t\}\}$, and for every $v=p+q$ with $p\in P$, $q\in Q$ and every $k\ge1$,
$$A^k(p+q)=B^k p+\bigl(\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{k-1}\bigr)\bigl(A(q)-q\bigr)+q .$$
3. **Exact order of the rank-two product.** For any distinct $s,t$ and the notation of (2), when $m<\infty$ put $\zeta:=\zeta_{st}$, of order $2m$, so $c=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$; when $m=\infty$ use $c=2$, with no $\zeta$ stipulated. Then:
   (a) if $2<m<\infty$, the characteristic polynomial of $B$ is $X^2-(c^2-2)X+1=(X-\zeta^2)(X-\zeta^{-2})$ with distinct roots; $B$ is diagonalisable, $B^m=\mathrm{id}_P$, $\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{m-1}=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for $0<k<m$;
   (b) if $m=2$, then $c=0$ and $B=-\mathrm{id}_P$;
   (c) if $m=\infty$, then $c=2$, $B\ne\mathrm{id}_P$, $(B-\mathrm{id}_P)^2=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for every $k\ge1$.
   Hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=A$ has order exactly $m$ when $m<\infty$, and infinite order when $m=\infty$; in particular $A^m=\mathrm{id}_E$ and $A^k\ne\mathrm{id}_E$ for $0<k<m$ in the finite case.
4. **The representation and the exact dihedral orders.** The assignment $s\mapsto\sigma_s$ respects every defining relator of $W$ and induces a unique homomorphism $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ with $\sigma(s)=\sigma_s$. Consequently, for any distinct $s,t\in S$, one has $s\ne t$ in $W$ and $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$ (infinite when $m(s,t)=\infty$).
5. **The signed reflection action.** Let $T:=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}\subseteq W$. For $s\in S$ define $U_s:\{\pm1\}\times T\to\{\pm1\}\times T$ by
$$U_s(\varepsilon,r):=\bigl(\varepsilon\cdot(-1)^{\delta(s,r)},\ srs\bigr),$$
where $\delta(s,r)=1$ if $r=s$ and $\delta(s,r)=0$ otherwise. Then $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ for every $s$, and the assignment $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot s:=U_s(\varepsilon,r)$ extends to a well-defined **right action** of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ (so $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot1=(\varepsilon,r)$ and $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(wv)=((\varepsilon,r)\cdot w)\cdot v$). Let $S$ be any set, possibly infinite, and let $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be a Coxeter matrix: $m(s,s)=1$, and for distinct $s,t$, $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$. Let $F(S)$ be the free group on $S$, let $N$ be the normal closure of
$$
\{s^2:s\in S\}\cup\{(st)^{m(s,t)}:s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty\},
$$
and define $W=F(S)/N$. The image of $s\in S$ in $W$ is also denoted $s$. This is the Coxeter group presented by $(S,m)$.

For $w\in W$, define its length by
$$
\ell(w)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N: w=s_1\cdots s_k\text{ for some }s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\}.
$$
The set is nonempty because every element of the quotient has a finite word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ and the relators give $s^{-1}=s$; its minimum exists by the well-ordering principle. A word of length $\ell(w)$ for $w$ is a reduced expression; the empty word is the reduced expression of $1$.

Define the reflection set $T=\{x s x^{-1}:x\in W,\ s\in S\}$. Write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for a reflection $t\in T$ and $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. Define the reflection-chain Bruhat order by $u\le v$ if there is a finite chain $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain is allowed. Length strictly increases on each nonempty chain, so this relation is a partial order. The exact reduced-subword description and finite-interval consequence needed below are established in [[thm-arbitrary-rank-finite-parabolics-and-bruhat-subword]].

When $S$ is finite, the presentation and length agree with [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and the reflection-chain order agrees with [[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]. No exchange, standard-parabolic, reduced-subword, or interval-finiteness property is included in this definition; those properties are justified separately.

Let $(W,S)$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. A **totally ordered abelian group** $(\Gamma,+,0,<)$ is an abelian group with a total order invariant under translation. Its group algebra $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ consists of finite sums $\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}a_\gamma v^\gamma$, where $a_\gamma\in\mathbb Z$, with $v^\gamma v^\delta=v^{\gamma+\delta}$. Define the ring involution $\overline{v^\gamma}=v^{-\gamma}$, and set
$$
A_{<0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma<0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma,\qquad A_{\le0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma\le0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma.
$$

A **weight function** is a map $L:W\to\Gamma$ such that $L(xy)=L(x)+L(y)$ whenever $\ell(xy)=\ell(x)+\ell(y)$. Its simple-generator parameters are $L(s)$ for $s\in S$. The exact criterion for prescribing those values on the simple generators is proved in [[lem-simple-generator-weights-extend-to-a-weight-function]]. No sign restriction on $L(s)$ is part of this definition.

The coefficient ordering used on the weighted Kazhdan–Lusztig basis is the given order on $\Gamma$, through $A_{<0}$. The group algebra elements $v^{L(s)}$ are units for every $s\in S$.

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter matrix $m$, let $(W,S)$ be the presented system of [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]], and let $\Gamma$ be the ordered abelian group of [[def-unequal-parameter-weight-function-and-coefficient-order]]. Every weight function $L:W\to\Gamma$ has $L(s)=L(t)$ whenever $s\ne t$, $m(s,t)<\infty$, and $m(s,t)$ is odd. Conversely, every label map $\lambda:S\to\Gamma$ satisfying these odd-edge equalities extends uniquely to a weight function with $L(s)=\lambda(s)$.

Let $(W,S)$, $\Gamma$, $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$, and $L:W\to\Gamma$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]] and [[def-unequal-parameter-weight-function-and-coefficient-order]]. For $s\in S$, write $q_s=v^{L(s)}\in A^\times$. Let $F=A\langle T_s:s\in S\rangle$ be the free associative $A$-algebra and let $I$ be the two-sided ideal generated by
$$
(T_s-q_s)(T_s+q_s^{-1})\quad(s\in S)
$$
and, for each distinct $s,t\in S$ with finite $m(s,t)$, the equality of the two alternating products of $T_s,T_t$ having $m(s,t)$ factors. Define the **unequal-parameter Coxeter Hecke algebra** by $H_A(W,L)=F/I$, and use $T_s$ for the image of a generator. For $m(s,t)=\infty$ there is no braid relation between $T_s$ and $T_t$.

The quadratic relation is equivalently
$$
T_s^2=(q_s-q_s^{-1})T_s+1,
$$
so each $T_s$ is invertible with $T_s^{-1}=T_s-(q_s-q_s^{-1})$. The basis, bar, and Bruhat support properties are not part of this definition; they are proved in [[lem-unequal-parameter-hecke-standard-basis-and-bar-triangularity]].

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter matrix $m$, and let $W,\ell,T,\le$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. For a finite $J\subseteq S$, let $W_J^*$ be the group presented by the restricted matrix $m|_J$, and let $\phi_J:W_J^*\to W$ send each generator to the same-named element.

1. The map $\phi_J$ is injective with image $\langle J\rangle$, and intrinsic length in $W_J^*$ equals ambient length in $W$ on this subgroup.
2. For $y,w\in W$, $y\le w$ if and only if a reduced expression of $y$ occurs as a subword of any fixed reduced expression of $w$. In particular, the interval $\{y:y\le w\}$ is finite and has at most $2^{\ell(w)}$ elements.
3. For every $s\in S$ and $w\in W$, $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)\pm1$ and $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; let $R$, $v_s$, $H$, $T_s$ be as in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]; let $T_w$ for $w\in W$ and the spanning statement be as in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]]; and let $E$, $P_s$, $Q_s$ and $P_w$ be as in [[lem-hh-commuting-left-right-hecke-length-operators]].

1. **The length-operator representation.** There is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\rho:H\to\operatorname{End}_R(E)$ with $\rho(T_s)=P_s$ for all $s\in S$; it satisfies $\rho(T_w)=P_w$ and $\rho(T_w)(e_1)=e_w$ for all $w\in W$.
2. **Standard basis.** $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ is an $R$-basis of $H$: it spans by [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]] and is $R$-linearly independent. Hence $H$ is free as an $R$-module and every element of $H$ has a unique expansion $\sum_wa_wT_w$ with $a_w\in R$ and all but finitely many $a_w$ zero.
3. **Faithfulness.** $\rho$ is injective.
4. **Base change.** For every commutative ring $R'$ and every ring homomorphism $\varphi:R\to R'$, the scalar extension $R'\otimes_RH$ is, as an $R'$-algebra, canonically isomorphic to the quotient of the free associative $R'$-algebra on $(T_s)_{s\in S}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the images under $\varphi$ of the relations (Q) and (B) of [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]], and it is free as an $R'$-module with basis $(1\otimes T_w)_{w\in W}$. No flatness or freeness of $R'$ over $R$ is assumed, and no torsion-freeness or semisimplicity of $H$ or of its specialisations is claimed.

Let $w\in W$ have reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_q$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]) and let $\le$ be the Bruhat order ([[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]).

**(1) Subword criterion.** For every $u\in W$,
$$u\le w\iff\text{there exist }1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le q\text{ with }u=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k},$$
and the indices may be chosen with $k=\ell(u)$, so that $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ is then a reduced expression of $u$.

**(2) Expression independence.** For all $u,w\in W$ the following are equivalent: (a) $u\le w$; (b) every reduced expression of $w$ has a subword that is a reduced expression of $u$; (c) some reduced expression of $w$ has a subword that is a reduced expression of $u$.

**(3) The identity.** In particular $1\le w$ for every $w\in W$: the empty subword of any reduced expression realizes the identity.

derivations.claim: **Finite-support spanning.** Fix a finite $J\subseteq S$. Its odd-edge components have a universal Laurent coefficient ring with one unit parameter for each component. By [F2], sending that parameter to $v^{L(s)}\in A^\times$ is independent of $s$ in the component, so it defines a coefficient-ring homomorphism. By [F4] and [F5], the finite Hecke algebra on $J$, after this base change, has basis $\{T_u:u\in W_J\}$. Every word representing an element of the global presented algebra uses some finite $J$, so applying this finite spanning statement to that word shows that the global elements $T_w$ span $H_A(W,L)$.

**The bar automorphism.** The quadratic relation in [F3] gives $T_s^{-1}=T_s-(q_s-q_s^{-1})$, where $q_s=v^{L(s)}$. Define a semilinear multiplicative map on the free algebra by $v^\gamma\mapsto v^{-\gamma}$ and $T_s\mapsto T_s^{-1}$. The image of a quadratic relator is $(T_s^{-1}-q_s^{-1})(T_s^{-1}+q_s)$, which is zero because multiplying $T_s^2-(q_s-q_s^{-1})T_s-1=0$ by $T_s^{-2}$ gives that same identity. The image of a braid relation is the inverse of the reversed alternating relation; reversal of either alternating word is one of the two defining alternating words, so the relation is preserved. The map descends to $H_A(W,L)$. Its square fixes every coefficient and every $T_s$, hence is the identity.

**Independence by finite support.** Suppose a finite sum $\sum_{w\in F}a_wT_w$ is zero in $H_A(W,L)$. In the free associative presentation, a representative belongs to the two-sided ideal generated by the quadratic and braid relations. Such membership is a finite sum of products of generators and relations, so only finitely many simple generators occur in that expression and in the reduced words for $w\in F$. Put them in a finite set $J$. The same relation then holds in the finite Hecke presentation on $J$, where [F5] gives independence of its standard basis. Thus every $a_w=0$. Together with step 1.1 this proves that $\{T_w\}$ is an $A$-basis and that the reduced product $T_w$ is independent of the chosen expression.

**Multiplication by a simple generator.** By [F4], exactly one of $\ell(sx)=\ell(x)+1$ and $\ell(sx)=\ell(x)-1$ holds. In the first case, a reduced word for $x$ prefixed by $s$ is reduced, so $T_sT_x=T_{sx}$. In the second, $x=s(sx)$ is reduced and the quadratic relation gives $T_sT_x=T_{sx}+(q_s-q_s^{-1})T_x$. Thus, when a simple letter is prepended to a standard-basis term, each output label is either the value with that letter prepended or the value with that letter omitted.

**Bruhat support.** Write a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_k$. Then $\overline{T_w}=T_{s_1}^{-1}\cdots T_{s_k}^{-1}$. Expanding each inverse as $T_{s_i}-(q_{s_i}-q_{s_i}^{-1})$ gives scalar multiples of products along subwords. Build each selected product from its rightmost letter toward its left; at each multiplication step 3.1 shows that its standard-basis labels are still values of subwords of the original reduced expression. By [F4] and [F6], each such label $y$ satisfies $y\le w$. A proper subword has length at most $k-1$, so it cannot equal $w$; the full reduced word contributes $T_w$ with coefficient one. Hence $\overline{T_w}-T_w$ is supported strictly below $w$.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove the standard-basis clause, step 1.2 constructs the involution, and step 4.1 proves its strict Bruhat support. All reductions take place in finite supports, so no finite-rank hypothesis or choice axiom is used.

Their triangular expansions show that the $C_y$ form an $A$-basis of $V_{<w}:=\operatorname{span}_A\{T_y:y<w\}$: the transition matrix is finite, unitriangular, and ordered by length.

Set $D_w=\overline{T_w}-T_w$. By [F2], there are unique coefficients $a_y\in A$ with $D_w=\sum_{y<w}a_yC_y$. The basis property in step 1.1 gives $\overline{a_y}=-a_y$ for each $y<w$.

Write $a_y=\sum_{\gamma}n_\gamma v^\gamma$ with finite support. The equality $\overline{a_y}=-a_y$ forces $n_0=0$ and $n_{-\gamma}=-n_\gamma$. Let $p_y=\sum_{\gamma<0}n_\gamma v^\gamma\in A_{<0}$; then $p_y-\overline{p_y}=a_y$. Define $C_w=T_w+\sum_{y<w}p_yC_y$. The associated left cell quotient, right cell quotient, and two-sided cell quotient are respectively $I^L_{\le\mathcal C}/I^L_{<\mathcal C}$, $I^R_{\le\mathcal C}/I^R_{<\mathcal C}$, and $I^{LR}_{\le\mathcal C}/I^{LR}_{<\mathcal C}$. [[thm-unequal-parameter-cell-quotients-are-modules]] proves that these quotients inherit the stated module or bimodule actions and have bases indexed by their cells.

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter group $W$, let $L:W\to\Gamma$ be any weight function into a totally ordered abelian group, let $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$, and let $H_A(W,L)$ and its bar involution be as above. For each $w\in W$, there is a unique element $C_w\in H_A(W,L)$ such that
$$
\overline{C_w}=C_w,\qquad C_w=T_w+\sum_{y<w}p_{y,w}T_y,\qquad p_{y,w}\in A_{<0}.
$$
The family $\{C_w:w\in W\}$ is an $A$-basis. For a simple generator $s$ the normalization is
$$C_s=\begin{cases}T_s+v^{-L(s)},&L(s)>0,\\T_s,&L(s)=0,\\T_s-v^{L(s)},&L(s)<0.\end{cases}$$

derivations.claim: **The left spans are left ideals.** If $C_x$ occurs in $C_sC_y$, then $x\leftarrow_L y$, hence $x\le_L y$. Therefore, if $y\le_L\mathcal C$, every basis term in $C_sC_y$ also has index $\le_L\mathcal C$, proving closure of $I^L_{\le\mathcal C}$ under left multiplication by each $C_s$. If $y<_{L}\mathcal C$, each such $x$ is also outside $\mathcal C$: otherwise some $g\in\mathcal C$ satisfies $g\le_L x\le_L y\le_L g$, forcing $y\in\mathcal C$, a contradiction. Thus $I^L_{<\mathcal C}$ is also closed under left multiplication by each $C_s$. Since $T_s=C_s-\eta_s$, the $C_s$ and scalars generate $H_A(W,L)$, so both spans are left ideals.

**The right spans are right ideals.** If $C_x$ occurs in $C_yC_s$, then $x\leftarrow_R y$, hence $x\le_R y$. Thus right multiplication by each $C_s$ preserves the right numerator. If $y$ is in the right denominator and $x\in\mathcal C$, choose $g\in\mathcal C$ with $y\le_R g$; since $g$ and $x$ lie in the same cell, $g\le_R x$, while $x\le_R y$. Transitivity would make $g$ equivalent to $y$, contradicting $y\notin\mathcal C$. So right multiplication also preserves the right denominator. The generators $T_s=C_s-\eta_s$ then show that these spans are right ideals of $H_A(W,L)$.

**The two-sided spans are two-sided ideals.** A two-sided preorder step is a left step or a right step. Applying the closure arguments of steps 1.1 and 1.2 to each type of step shows that left and right multiplication by every $C_s$, and hence by every $T_s$, preserves both $I^{LR}_{\le\mathcal C}$ and $I^{LR}_{<\mathcal C}$. They are therefore two-sided ideals.

**Quotient bases and actions.** The KL basis is an $A$-basis by [F2]. For the corresponding preorder, every $x\in\mathcal C$ belongs to the numerator because $x\le x$; every numerator index outside $\mathcal C$ belongs to the denominator by its definition. Thus the numerator basis indices are the disjoint union of the cell $\mathcal C$ and the denominator indices, so their quotient has basis exactly the images of $C_w$ with $w\in\mathcal C$. The induced left, right, or bimodule action is well defined because the numerator and denominator are ideals of the required sidedness, as proved in steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1.

citations.quote:
Let $S$ be any set, possibly infinite, and let $m:S\times S\to\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be a Coxeter matrix: $m(s,s)=1$, and for distinct $s,t$, $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$. Let $F(S)$ be the free group on $S$, let $N$ be the normal closure of
$$
\{s^2:s\in S\}\cup\{(st)^{m(s,t)}:s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty\},
$$
and define $W=F(S)/N$. The image of $s\in S$ in $W$ is also denoted $s$. This is the Coxeter group presented by $(S,m)$.

For $w\in W$, define its length by
$$
\ell(w)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N: w=s_1\cdots s_k\text{ for some }s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\}.
$$
The set is nonempty because every element of the quotient has a finite word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ and the relators give $s^{-1}=s$; its minimum exists by the well-ordering principle. A word of length $\ell(w)$ for $w$ is a reduced expression; the empty word is the reduced expression of $1$.

Define the reflection set $T=\{x s x^{-1}:x\in W,\ s\in S\}$. Write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for a reflection $t\in T$ and $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. Define the reflection-chain Bruhat order by $u\le v$ if there is a finite chain $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain is allowed. Length strictly increases on each nonempty chain, so this relation is a partial order. The exact reduced-subword description and finite-interval consequence needed below are established in [[thm-arbitrary-rank-finite-parabolics-and-bruhat-subword]].

When $S$ is finite, the presentation and length agree with [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and the reflection-chain order agrees with [[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]. No exchange, standard-parabolic, reduced-subword, or interval-finiteness property is included in this definition; those properties are justified separately.

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter matrix $m$, and let $W,\ell,T,\le$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. For a finite $J\subseteq S$, let $W_J^*$ be the group presented by the restricted matrix $m|_J$, and let $\phi_J:W_J^*\to W$ send each generator to the same-named element.

1. The map $\phi_J$ is injective with image $\langle J\rangle$, and intrinsic length in $W_J^*$ equals ambient length in $W$ on this subgroup.
2. For $y,w\in W$, $y\le w$ if and only if a reduced expression of $y$ occurs as a subword of any fixed reduced expression of $w$. In particular, the interval $\{y:y\le w\}$ is finite and has at most $2^{\ell(w)}$ elements.
3. For every $s\in S$ and $w\in W$, $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)\pm1$ and $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$.

Let $(W,S)$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]]. A **totally ordered abelian group** $(\Gamma,+,0,<)$ is an abelian group with a total order invariant under translation. Its group algebra $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$ consists of finite sums $\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}a_\gamma v^\gamma$, where $a_\gamma\in\mathbb Z$, with $v^\gamma v^\delta=v^{\gamma+\delta}$. Define the ring involution $\overline{v^\gamma}=v^{-\gamma}$, and set
$$
A_{<0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma<0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma,\qquad A_{\le0}=\bigoplus_{\gamma\le0}\mathbb Z v^\gamma.
$$

A **weight function** is a map $L:W\to\Gamma$ such that $L(xy)=L(x)+L(y)$ whenever $\ell(xy)=\ell(x)+\ell(y)$. Its simple-generator parameters are $L(s)$ for $s\in S$. The exact criterion for prescribing those values on the simple generators is proved in [[lem-simple-generator-weights-extend-to-a-weight-function]]. No sign restriction on $L(s)$ is part of this definition.

The coefficient ordering used on the weighted Kazhdan–Lusztig basis is the given order on $\Gamma$, through $A_{<0}$. The group algebra elements $v^{L(s)}$ are units for every $s\in S$.

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter matrix $m$, let $(W,S)$ be the presented system of [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]], and let $\Gamma$ be the ordered abelian group of [[def-unequal-parameter-weight-function-and-coefficient-order]]. Every weight function $L:W\to\Gamma$ has $L(s)=L(t)$ whenever $s\ne t$, $m(s,t)<\infty$, and $m(s,t)$ is odd. Conversely, every label map $\lambda:S\to\Gamma$ satisfying these odd-edge equalities extends uniquely to a weight function with $L(s)=\lambda(s)$.

Let $(W,S)$, $\Gamma$, $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$, and $L:W\to\Gamma$ be as in [[def-arbitrary-rank-coxeter-system-and-bruhat-order]] and [[def-unequal-parameter-weight-function-and-coefficient-order]]. For $s\in S$, write $q_s=v^{L(s)}\in A^\times$. Let $F=A\langle T_s:s\in S\rangle$ be the free associative $A$-algebra and let $I$ be the two-sided ideal generated by
$$
(T_s-q_s)(T_s+q_s^{-1})\quad(s\in S)
$$
and, for each distinct $s,t\in S$ with finite $m(s,t)$, the equality of the two alternating products of $T_s,T_t$ having $m(s,t)$ factors. Define the **unequal-parameter Coxeter Hecke algebra** by $H_A(W,L)=F/I$, and use $T_s$ for the image of a generator. For $m(s,t)=\infty$ there is no braid relation between $T_s$ and $T_t$.

The quadratic relation is equivalently
$$
T_s^2=(q_s-q_s^{-1})T_s+1,
$$
so each $T_s$ is invertible with $T_s^{-1}=T_s-(q_s-q_s^{-1})$. The basis, bar, and Bruhat support properties are not part of this definition; they are proved in [[lem-unequal-parameter-hecke-standard-basis-and-bar-triangularity]].

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter group $W$, let $L:W\to\Gamma$ be a weight function as in [[def-unequal-parameter-weight-function-and-coefficient-order]], and let $H_A(W,L)$ be as in [[def-unequal-parameter-coxeter-hecke-algebra]]. Then:

1. For each $w$, the product $T_w$ along a reduced expression is independent of the chosen expression, and $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_A(W,L)$.
2. The assignments $\overline{v^\gamma}=v^{-\gamma}$ and $\overline{T_s}=T_s^{-1}$ extend to an involutive semilinear algebra automorphism of $H_A(W,L)$.
3. For every reduced expression of $w$, the expansion of $\overline{T_w}-T_w$ in the standard basis is supported on $T_y$ with $y<w$ in Bruhat order.

Let $S$ be any set with Coxeter group $W$, let $L:W\to\Gamma$ be any weight function into a totally ordered abelian group, let $A=\mathbb Z[\Gamma]$, and let $H_A(W,L)$ and its bar involution be as above. For each $w\in W$, there is a unique element $C_w\in H_A(W,L)$ such that
$$
\overline{C_w}=C_w,\qquad C_w=T_w+\sum_{y<w}p_{y,w}T_y,\qquad p_{y,w}\in A_{<0}.
$$
The family $\{C_w:w\in W\}$ is an $A$-basis. For a simple generator $s$ the normalization is
$$C_s=\begin{cases}T_s+v^{-L(s)},&L(s)>0,\\T_s,&L(s)=0,\\T_s-v^{L(s)},&L(s)<0.\end{cases}$$

Let $C_w$ be the basis of [[thm-unequal-parameter-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. For $x,y\in W$, write $x\leftarrow_L y$ if the coefficient of $C_x$ in $C_sC_y$ is nonzero for some $s\in S$. Write $x\le_L y$ if there is a finite chain $x=w_0,\ldots,w_n=y$ with $w_i\leftarrow_L w_{i+1}$ at every step. Define $x\leftarrow_R y$ from the coefficient of $C_x$ in $C_yC_s$, and define $\le_R$ by finite chains of such steps. Define $x\le_{LR}y$ by finite chains in which each step is either a left or a right step. The length-zero chain makes each relation reflexive, and concatenation makes each transitive. Mutual comparability defines equivalence relations; their classes are the left, right, and two-sided **cells**.

For a left cell $\mathcal C$, define
$$I^L_{\le\mathcal C}=\operatorname{span}_A\{C_x:x\le_L y\text{ for some }y\in\mathcal C\},\qquad I^L_{<\mathcal C}=\operatorname{span}_A\{C_x:x\le_L y\text{ for some }y\in\mathcal C,\ x\notin\mathcal C\}.$$
Define $I^R_{\le\mathcal C}, I^R_{<\mathcal C}$ for a right cell and $I^{LR}_{\le\mathcal C}, I^{LR}_{<\mathcal C}$ for a two-sided cell in the same way, using the corresponding preorder. The associated left cell quotient, right cell quotient, and two-sided cell quotient are respectively $I^L_{\le\mathcal C}/I^L_{<\mathcal C}$, $I^R_{\le\mathcal C}/I^R_{<\mathcal C}$, and $I^{LR}_{\le\mathcal C}/I^{LR}_{<\mathcal C}$. [[thm-unequal-parameter-cell-quotients-are-modules]] proves that these quotients inherit the stated module or bimodule actions and have bases indexed by their cells.

For every Coxeter system and weight function of [[def-unequal-parameter-coxeter-hecke-algebra]], the spans $I^L_{\le\mathcal C}$ and $I^L_{<\mathcal C}$ attached to a left cell are left ideals; the right-cell spans are right ideals; and the two-sided-cell spans are two-sided ideals. Therefore the quotients defined in [[def-unequal-parameter-cells-and-cell-quotients]] are left modules, right modules, or bimodules, respectively. Each quotient has an $A$-basis consisting exactly of the images of the KL basis elements indexed by its cell. No further cell property, semisimplicity, or irreducible-module classification is asserted.

Let $O$ be a Noetherian commutative local domain, with fraction field $K$, maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and residue field $k_0=O/\mathfrak m$. Allow a specified field extension $k/k_0$ as the specialization field. The nonfield DVR case is included: a nonfield discrete valuation ring is equivalently a local PID with nonzero maximal ideal ([[thm-equivalent-characterisations-of-a-dvr]]); the original residue-field specialization is $k=k_0$. Let $H_O$ be a finite free $O$-algebra, so it has finite rank as an $O$-module. Assume the generic algebra $H_K=K\otimes_O H_O$ is split semisimple, meaning a finite product of full matrix algebras over $K$; assume $H_k=k\otimes_O H_O$ is split, meaning each simple module remains simple after extending the field. A simple module is a nonzero module with no proper nonzero submodule. Write $\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$ and $\operatorname{Irr}(H_k)$ for their isomorphism classes of simple modules. For each $E\in\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$, choose an $H_O$-stable $O$-lattice $\Lambda_E\subset E$, meaning a finite free $O$-submodule spanning $E$ over $K$. Assume each simple $M\in\operatorname{Irr}(H_k)$ occurs in at least one reduction $k\otimes_{k_0}(\Lambda_E/\mathfrak m\Lambda_E)$, so every column below is nonzero. For such $M$, let
$$
d_{E,M}=[k\otimes_{k_0}(\Lambda_E/\mathfrak m\Lambda_E):M]
$$
be the multiplicity of $M$ among the composition factors of this finite-dimensional $H_k$-module. A composition series is a finite strict submodule chain with simple successive quotients; one exists by induction on module dimension, and Jordan–Hölder makes its multiplicities independent of the chosen series ([[def-composition-series-and-composition-factors-of-an-object]], [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-in-an-abelian-category]]). The matrix $D=(d_{E,M})$ is the decomposition matrix for these chosen lattices. This definition makes no choice-independence assertion for arbitrary local orders. The finite-Weyl theorem below supplies free integral models and proves their multiplicities independent in its complete local setting; the rank-one worked specialization gives its lattices directly.

Fix an integer-valued statistic $\alpha_E$ on $\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$. In Geck's finite-Weyl Hecke convention this is the Schur-element exponent denoted $\alpha_E$; its particular values do not enter the identity-matrix case. Put
$$
\check\alpha_M=\min\{\alpha_E:d_{E,M}>0\}.
$$
A subset $B\subseteq\operatorname{Irr}(H_K)$ is a **canonical basic set** (relative to $D$ and $\alpha$) if there is a bijection $M\mapsto E(M)$ from $\operatorname{Irr}(H_k)$ to $B$ satisfying
$$
d_{E(M),M}=1,\qquad \alpha_{E(M)}=\check\alpha_M,
$$
and, for every $E,M$,
$$
d_{E,M}>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \check\alpha_M<\alpha_E\ \text{or}\ E=E(M).
$$
This is a definition only; it makes no claim that such a subset exists in every specialization.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $R$, $H$, and $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]], and [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], and assume $W$ is finite. For the unique standard-basis expansion $h=\sum_{w\in W}r_wT_w$, define the **canonical Hecke trace**
$$
\tau:H\to R,\qquad \tau(h):=r_1.
$$

The associated $R$-bilinear form is $B_\tau(a,b):=\tau(ab)$. A trace is **symmetric** when $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for every $a,b\in H$. The form is **perfect** when the $R$-linear map
$$
H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(H,R),\qquad a\longmapsto[b\longmapsto\tau(ab)]
$$
is an isomorphism. A **symmetrizing trace** is a trace for which this form is symmetric and perfect. This is an integral definition over $R$; it assumes no field, semisimplicity, or nondegeneracy after passing to a fraction field. The theorem [[thm-hh-canonical-hecke-trace-is-symmetric-and-perfect]] proves these properties for $\tau$ and every commutative base change of $R$.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $R$, $H$, the standard basis $\{T_w:w\in W\}$, and the trace $\tau$ be as in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]], [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], and [[def-hh-canonical-hecke-trace-and-symmetrizing-form]]. Assume $W$ is finite. On the finite free $R$-module $E=\bigoplus_{w\in W}Re_w$, define the coordinate pairing by $\langle e_x,e_y\rangle=\delta_{x,y}$ and extend $R$-bilinearly. For an endomorphism $A$ with $A(e_x)=\sum_y a_{y,x}e_y$, define its coordinate transpose by $A^t(e_y)=\sum_xa_{y,x}e_x$, so $\langle Au,v\rangle=\langle u,A^tv\rangle$. Let $P_s$ be the left length operator of [[lem-hh-commuting-left-right-hecke-length-operators]].

For all $x,y\in W$,
$$
\tau(T_xT_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y}.
$$
Consequently $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for all $a,b\in H$, and the map $H\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(H,R)$, $a\mapsto[b\mapsto\tau(ab)]$, is an isomorphism. The basis dual to $\{T_w:w\in W\}$ for this pairing is $\{T_{w^{-1}}:w\in W\}$; it is the standard basis indexed by inverses, not the algebra-inverse family $\{T_w^{-1}\}$.

For every unital homomorphism of commutative rings $\phi:R\to R'$, the induced canonical trace on $R'\otimes_RH$ has the same basis-pair formula and is again symmetric and perfect. No semisimplicity, field, or nondegeneracy hypothesis is required.

Let $K$ be a field and $H$ a finite-dimensional split semisimple $K$-algebra, meaning $H\cong\prod_{i=1}^n M_{d_i}(K)$ for positive integers $d_i$. Let $\tau:H\to K$ be a symmetrizing trace: $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$, and the bilinear form $(a,b)\mapsto\tau(ab)$ is nondegenerate. For each simple $H$-module $E$, let $\chi_E(h)=\operatorname{Tr}_K(h|_E)$ be its character. If the trace has an expansion
$$
\tau=\sum_{E\in\operatorname{Irr}(H)}c_E^{-1}\chi_E
$$
with all $c_E\in K^\times$, the scalars $c_E$ are the **Schur elements** of the pair $(H,\tau)$. The definition makes no existence claim for an arbitrary functional; existence and values require a separate proof in the specified regime. The rank-one specialization computes them directly, while the finite-Weyl asymptotic theorem proves the full trace expansion and its leading coefficients.

For the canonical finite Coxeter Hecke trace and its symmetric perfect pairing, see [[def-hh-canonical-hecke-trace-and-symmetrizing-form]] and [[thm-hh-canonical-hecke-trace-is-symmetric-and-perfect]].

derivations.claim: From $(st)^2=1$ and $s^2=t^2=1$, $st=(st)^{-1}=ts$. Thus every word reduces to one of $1,s,t,st$. The homomorphism to $(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2$ sending $s\mapsto(1,0)$, $t\mapsto(0,1)$ respects all relators and separates these four elements, so they are distinct. Their lengths are $0,1,1,2$, respectively. Since the only finite edge has even label $2$, the odd-edge condition in [F2] permits the unequal labels $1,2$; it gives a well-defined weight function $L$.

Put $C_1=1$, $C_s=T_s+v^{-1}$, and $C_t=T_t+v^{-2}$. The rank-two relations give $T_s^2=(v-v^{-1})T_s+1$ and $T_t^2=(v^2-v^{-2})T_t+1$, so direct expansion gives $C_s^2=(v+v^{-1})C_s$ and $C_t^2=(v^2+v^{-2})C_t$. The generators commute because $m(s,t)=2$, and $C_{st}:=C_sC_t=C_tC_s=T_{st}+v^{-2}T_s+v^{-1}T_t+v^{-3}$. These elements are bar invariant and have leading standard term $T_w$ with lower Bruhat support and negative coefficients; uniqueness in [F4] identifies them as the KL basis.

For $r\in\{s,t\}$, set $a_s=q$, $a_t=q^2$. The specialized quadratic relation is $(T_r-a_r)(T_r+a_r^{-1})=0$. Since $a_r+a_r^{-1}\equiv2\pmod p$, it is a unit in $O$, so $e_r^+=(T_r+a_r^{-1})/(a_r+a_r^{-1})$ and $e_r^-=(a_r-T_r)/(a_r+a_r^{-1})$ belong to $H_O$. They sum to $1$, their product is zero by the quadratic relation, and $(T_r-a_r)e_r^+=(T_r+a_r^{-1})e_r^-=0$, so they are complementary idempotents. Every rank-one element $b+cT_r$ equals $(b+ca_r)e_r^+ +(b-ca_r^{-1})e_r^-$, making both summands free of rank one. The commuting rank-one subalgebras tensor to $H_O$ with the standard rank-four basis [F3], so the four products $e_s^\epsilon e_t^\delta$ give $H_O\cong O^4$ and hence $H_K\cong K^4$, $H_k\cong k^4$.

The complete left-product table is determined by $C_sC_1=C_s$, $C_tC_1=C_t$, $C_s^2=(v+v^{-1})C_s$, $C_tC_s=C_{st}$, $C_sC_t=C_{st}$, $C_t^2=(v^2+v^{-2})C_t$, $C_sC_{st}=C_s^2C_t=(v+v^{-1})C_{st}$, and $C_tC_{st}=C_sC_t^2=(v^2+v^{-2})C_{st}$. The right table is identical because the algebra is commutative. With an arrow $y\to x$ when $C_x$ occurs in $C_rC_y$ or $C_yC_r$, the only non-loop arrows are $1\to s$, $1\to t$, $s\to st$, and $t\to st$. No transition points back, so mutual comparability has four singleton classes for each left, right, and two-sided preorder.

In the quotient for $\{1\}$, both $C_s$ and $C_t$ vanish, so $T_s=C_s-v^{-1}$ and $T_t=C_t-v^{-2}$ act by $-v^{-1}$ and $-v^{-2}$. In the quotient for $\{s\}$, $C_tC_s=C_{st}$ vanishes while $C_s^2=(v+v^{-1})C_s$; hence $(T_s,T_t)$ acts by $(v,-v^{-2})$. In the quotient for $\{t\}$, $C_sC_t=C_{st}$ vanishes, so $T_s$ acts by $-v^{-1}$; $C_t^2=(v^2+v^{-2})C_t$ gives $T_t$-eigenvalue $v^2$. In the quotient for $\{st\}$, $C_sC_{st}=(v+v^{-1})C_{st}$ and $C_tC_{st}=(v^2+v^{-2})C_{st}$, so the action is $(v,v^2)$. By [F5] each is a well-defined one-dimensional cell module. Their four eigenvalue pairs are distinct over $K$, since $q+q^{-1}\ne0$ and $q^2+q^{-2}\ne0$ in the characteristic-zero field $K$.

The four cell characters from step 4.1 take values in $O$, so $\Lambda=O$ with the displayed scalar actions is an $H_O$-stable rank-one lattice for each. Their reductions have $T_s,T_t$ eigenvalues respectively $(-1,-1)$, $(1,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, and $(1,1)$ in $k$. Since $p$ is odd these are four distinct characters of $H_k\cong k^4$; each is simple, and each reduced lattice has composition multiplicity one for exactly its matching character. Thus $D=I_4$, up to ordering.

Let $K_0=\mathbb Q(v)$ be the generic coefficient field and put $U_r=v^{L(r)}T_r$, which has eigenvalues $Q_r=v^{2L(r)}$ and $-1$. By [F7], the canonical trace on the normalized standard basis $U_w$ takes value $1$ on the identity and $0$ on nonidentity elements, and its generic pairing is symmetrizing. For one rank-one factor, the algebra over $K_0$ is $K_0\times K_0$, with characters $\chi_+(U_r)=Q_r$, $\chi_-(U_r)=-1$. By [F8], write $\tau=c_+^{-1}\chi_++c_-^{-1}\chi_-$. Evaluating at $1$ and $U_r$ gives $c_+^{-1}+c_-^{-1}=1$ and $Q_rc_+^{-1}-c_-^{-1}=0$; solving yields $c_+=1+Q_r$ and $c_-=1+Q_r^{-1}$. For $A_1\times A_1$, the algebra and trace are tensor products of the rank-one factors, so the four Schur elements are products of one term from $\{1+v^2,1+v^{-2}\}$ and one from $\{1+v^4,1+v^{-4}\}$. Under the residue map $v\mapsto1$ in $k$, each product is $4\ne0$. $$

For $w\in W$, define its length by
$$
\ell(w)=\min\{k\in\mathbb N: w=s_1\cdots s_k\text{ for some }s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\}.
$$
The set is nonempty because every element of the quotient has a finite word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ and the relators give $s^{-1}=s$; its minimum exists by the well-ordering principle. A word of length $\ell(w)$ for $w$ is a reduced expression; the empty word is the reduced expression of $1$.

Define the reflection set $T=\{x s x^{-1}:x\in W,\ s\in S\}$. Write $u\to v$ if $v=ut$ for a reflection $t\in T$ and $\ell(v)>\ell(u)$. Define the reflection-chain Bruhat order by $u\le v$ if there is a finite chain $u=u_0\to u_1\to\cdots\to u_k=v$; the empty chain is allowed. Length strictly increases on each nonempty chain, so this relation is a partial order. The exact reduced-subword description and finite-interval consequence needed below are established in [[thm-arbitrary-rank-finite-parabolics-and-bruhat-subword]].

When $S$ is finite, the presentation and length agree with [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], and the reflection-chain order agrees with [[def-cg-bruhat-order-by-reflection-chains]]. 1. The map $\phi_J$ is injective with image $\langle J\rangle$, and intrinsic length in $W_J^*$ equals ambient length in $W$ on this subgroup.
2. For $y,w\in W$, $y\le w$ if and only if a reduced expression of $y$ occurs as a subword of any fixed reduced expression of $w$. In particular, the interval $\{y:y\le w\}$ is finite and has at most $2^{\ell(w)}$ elements.

The standard basis and Bruhat subword property in [F1,F3] show triangularity with negative lower coefficients; bar invariance and uniqueness in [F3] identify the KL elements. The complete left products are $C_sC_1=C_s$, $C_tC_1=C_t$, $C_sC_s=(v+v^{-1})C_s$, $C_tC_s=C_{st}$, $C_sC_t=C_{st}$, $C_tC_t=(v^2+v^{-2})C_t$, $C_sC_{st}=C_s^2C_t=(v+v^{-1})C_{st}$, and $C_tC_{st}=C_sC_t^2=(v^2+v^{-2})C_{st}$. Right products agree because the algebra is commutative. Hence the only non-loop arrows are $1\to s$, $1\to t$, $s\to st$, and $t\to st$, so all four cells are singletons. In the $\{1\}$-quotient $C_s,C_t$ vanish, giving $(T_s,T_t)=(-v^{-1},-v^{-2})$; in the $\{s\}$-quotient $C_s^2$ gives $T_s=v$ and $C_tC_s=C_{st}$ vanishes, giving $T_t=-v^{-2}$; in the $\{t\}$-quotient $C_sC_t=C_{st}$ vanishes, giving $T_s=-v^{-1}$, and $C_t^2$ gives $T_t=v^2$; in the $\{st\}$-quotient the last two products give $(T_s,T_t)=(v,v^2)$. By [F4] these are well-defined cell modules, with exactly the four action pairs in the counterexample.

At $v=3$, the two possible $T_s$-eigenvalues $3,-3^{-1}$ are distinct in $K$, since $3+3^{-1}=10/3\ne0$. The two possible $T_t$-eigenvalues $3^2,-3^{-2}$ are distinct since $3^2+3^{-2}=82/9\ne0$. Thus the four pairs listed in this counterexample label four distinct one-dimensional simple $H_K$-modules. Each has an $O$-stable lattice $\Lambda=O$, because all four eigenvalues lie in $O$.

Each of the four lattices from step 3.1 reduces to the one-dimensional character $T_s=T_t=1$, which is the unique simple module found in step 2.1. Each reduction is itself simple, so its composition multiplicity is one. Hence the decomposition matrix has four rows and one column, all entries equal to $1$, by [F5]. The four generic labels have collapsed to one special simple label, proving the claimed failure of universal label preservation. This calculation does not decide whether some subset satisfies the canonical-basic-set conditions.

derivations.claim: Put $B=A_{\mathfrak p}$. It is a nonzero Noetherian local domain by [F1]. Its residue is $\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p)$: modulo $\mathfrak p$, the inverted elements are exactly the nonzero elements of $A/\mathfrak p$. This identifies that field with $k_0\subseteq k$. Localizing a domain is injective. The elementary prime correspondence used below follows directly from fractions: a prime disjoint from the denominators extends to a prime, and contraction recovers it because a fraction belongs to the extended ideal exactly when its numerator does.

If $\mathfrak p\cap\mathbb Z=0$, every nonzero integer is a unit in $B$, so fraction arithmetic identifies $B$ with a prime localization of $\mathbb Q[v,v^{-1}]$. The latter is a PID: ideals in its localization are generated by the image of a generator of their contracted ideal in $\mathbb Q[v]$. Thus $B$ is a field or has a nonzero principal maximal ideal $(a)$. In the second case [F2] and the chain $(0)\subsetneq(a)$ give dimension one. The class of $a$ modulo $(a)^2$ is nonzero, since $a=a^2b$ in the domain would imply $1=ab$ with $a$ a nonunit. Hence its embedding dimension is one. In the field case both dimensions are zero. Thus $B$ is regular in both cases.

Otherwise $\mathfrak p\cap\mathbb Z=(\ell)$ for a prime integer $\ell$. The prime $\mathfrak p/(\ell)$ in the PID $\mathbb F_\ell[v,v^{-1}]$ is zero or $(f)$ for an irreducible Laurent polynomial $f$. If it is zero, $\mathfrak p=(\ell)$ and the principal-maximal-ideal argument of step 2.1 proves regularity. Otherwise choose a Laurent lift $G$ of $f$; then the maximal ideal of $B$ is $\mathfrak m=(\ell,G)$. The chain $(0)\subsetneq(\ell)B\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ and [F2] give $\dim B=2$. The quotient $B/(\ell)$ is the domain $\mathbb F_\ell[v,v^{-1}]_{(f)}$. If $\ell=r\ell^2+s\ell G+tG^2$ in $B$, reduction modulo $\ell$ gives $\bar t f^2=0$, hence $t=\ell t'$. Cancellation of $\ell$ then gives $1=r\ell+sG+t'G^2\in\mathfrak m$, impossible. Thus $\ell\notin\mathfrak m^2$. If $a\ell+bG\in\mathfrak m^2$, reducing modulo $\ell$ gives $\bar b f\in(f^2)$, so $b\in\mathfrak m$. It follows that $a\ell\in\mathfrak m^2$, and $\ell\notin\mathfrak m^2$ forces $a\in\mathfrak m$, since otherwise $a$ is a unit. The two displayed generators therefore give a basis of $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$; its dimension is two. Thus $B$ is regular in this final case.

By [F3], $R=\widehat B$ is complete separated Noetherian local with residue $k_0$, is regular, and is a domain. Faithful flatness makes $B\to R$ injective: if $b$ maps to zero, flat tensoring the inclusion $bB\hookrightarrow B$ gives an injection $bB\otimes_B R\hookrightarrow R$ whose image is zero; faithfulness forces $bB=0$, so $b=0$. Therefore $A\hookrightarrow R$ induces $\mathbb Q(v)\hookrightarrow F$, with the required residue map. If $\mathfrak p=0$, this also covers the field $B=R=\mathbb Q(v)$ with zero maximal ideal.

For a finite projective module $P$ over any local ring, lift a basis of $P/\mathfrak mP$ to $r$ elements of $P$. Nakayama on the finite cokernel makes $R^r\to P$ surjective. Projectivity splits it as $R^r=P\oplus Q$, with $Q$ finite. Reduction of this direct sum shows $Q/\mathfrak mQ=0$, so Nakayama gives $Q=0$. Hence $P$ is free of rank $r$. Over our domain this rank equals both $\dim_F(F\otimes_RP)$ and $\dim_{k_0}(k_0\otimes_RP)$.

Let $x_0\in C$ lift an idempotent modulo $\mathfrak m_RC$. Define $\delta_i=x_i^2-x_i$ and $x_{i+1}=x_i+(1-2x_i)\delta_i$. All factors here are polynomials in $x_i$, so integer-polynomial expansion gives $\delta_{i+1}=\delta_i^2(4\delta_i-3)$. Thus $\delta_i\in\mathfrak m_R^{2^i}C$ and $x_{i+1}-x_i\in\mathfrak m_R^{2^i}C$. The finite-module completeness in [F4] gives a limit $q\equiv x_0$ modulo $\mathfrak m_RC$. Multiplication is continuous, since these ideal powers are two-sided ideals, so separatedness gives $q^2=q$. This construction involves no division and works in every characteristic.

For any right $C$-module $X$, the $R$-linear decomposition $X=Xq\oplus X(1-q)$ shows that projection $X\mapsto Xq$ commutes with every scalar extension. It is exact: under a surjection $X\to Y$, lift $y\in Y$ to $x$, and then $xq$ lifts $yq$; kernels and injections follow by restriction of the same projection. If $0\to I_{i+1}\to I_i\to B_i\to0$ is a filtration sequence, projection gives $0\to I_{i+1}q\to I_iq\to B_iq\to0$. When $B_i$ is finite free, $B_iq$ is finite projective and hence free by step 5.1; the sequence splits as $R$-modules. It therefore retains its exact layer after scalar extension, including reduction to $k_0$.

Finally let $J_R=\bigoplus_E M_{d_E}(R)$ act on an $R$-finite-free module $X$. With matrix units $e^E_{ij}$, put $Q_E=e^E_{11}X$. It is a direct summand of $X$, hence finite free by step 5.1. The map $R^{d_E}\otimes_RQ_E\to e_EX$ sending $u_i\otimes x$ to $e^E_{i1}x$ has inverse $y\mapsto\sum_i u_i\otimes e^E_{1i}y$, by the matrix-unit identities. Therefore the generic and residue multiplicities of the $E$-standard simple are both $\operatorname{rank}_RQ_E$. This proves the final assertion and completes the lemma.

The Laurent polynomial ring $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ of
[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]] is Noetherian, hence every ideal of
$\Lambda$ is finitely generated, and $\Lambda$ is a unique factorisation
domain; its units are $\pm t^k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and $t$ is prime in $\mathbb Z[t]$ but becomes a unit in $\Lambda$.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then

1. $R/I$ is Noetherian for every ideal $I$ of $R$
   ([[def-quotient-ring]]), and
2. $S^{-1}R$ is Noetherian for every multiplicative subset $S\subseteq R$
   ([[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).

Both cases include their degenerate instances: $I=R$ makes $R/I$ the zero ring,
and $0\in S$ makes $S^{-1}R$ the zero ring, and the zero ring is Noetherian.
For every field $F$, every ideal of $F[x]$ is generated by one polynomial; equivalently, $F[x]$ is a principal ideal domain.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let
$$ I=(x_1,\ldots,x_n) $$
be an ideal generated by $n\ge1$ elements, and let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal minimal over $I$. Then $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)\le n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring, and let $\widehat R$ be its
$\mathfrak m$-adic completion.

1. $\widehat R$ is a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal
   $\mathfrak m\widehat R$.
2. The residue field is unchanged:
   $$    \widehat R/\mathfrak m\widehat R \cong R/\mathfrak m.    $$
3. The completion map $R \to \widehat R$ is faithfully flat.
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A nonzero Noetherian local ring $R$ is regular if and only if its maximal-adic completion $\widehat R$ is regular.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$ is a domain and Cohen–Macaulay. For every regular system $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, the tuple is $R$-regular and $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is regular local of dimension $d-c$ for all $0\le c\le d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ satisfy $I \subseteq J(R)$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated left $R$-module. If $IM=M$, then $M=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $I \subseteq R$ be an ideal, and assume that
$R$ is $I$-adically complete. Then every finitely generated $R$-module $M$ is
$I$-adically complete.

derivations.claim: Reversing words gives the anti-involution $T_w\mapsto T_{w^{-1}}$ of the Hecke presentation. It commutes with bar. Inversion preserves length and sends a reflection-chain step $u\to ut$ to $u^{-1}\to tu^{-1}=u^{-1}(utu^{-1})$, again a length-increasing right-reflection step; hence it preserves Bruhat order. Thus it preserves Bruhat triangularity, and KL uniqueness gives $C_w\mapsto C_{w^{-1}}$. Hence $h_{x,y,z}=h_{y^{-1},x^{-1},z^{-1}}$, $a(z)=a(z^{-1})$, and $\gamma_{x,y,z}=\gamma_{y^{-1},x^{-1},z^{-1}}$. Comparing coefficients in the bar-invariant products $C_xC_y$ also gives $\overline{h_{x,y,z}}=h_{x,y,z}$. P3 with $y=1$ forces $a(1)=0$ and $1\in\mathcal D$, since $C_1C_1=C_1$ makes the required nonzero coefficient possible only for $d=1$ and exponent zero. The assignment $T_s\mapsto-T_s^{-1}$ preserves the quadratic relation and braid relations (the signs agree at equal braid length and inverse reversed braid words agree), is involutive and is $A$-linear. Thus $D_xD_y$ has the same constants $h$.

P8 implies that products in $J$ vanish across distinct $a$-degrees. For a fixed degree $i$, multiply P15′ by $v^i$ and take its constant coefficient. Whenever a $\gamma$ term is nonzero, P8 forces every participating index to have degree $i$. The resulting identity is $\sum_u\gamma_{x,u,y^{-1}}\gamma_{w,x',u^{-1}}=\sum_u\gamma_{x,w,u^{-1}}\gamma_{u,x',y^{-1}}$, exactly equality of the coefficients of $t_y$ in $t_x(t_wt_{x'})$ and $(t_xt_w)t_{x'}$. Other degree combinations vanish. This proves associativity without using any unlisted P property.

The coefficient of $t_y$ in $t_x\sum_dn_dt_d$ is $\sum_dn_d\gamma_{x,d,y^{-1}}=\sum_dn_d\gamma_{y^{-1},x,d}$ by P7. P2 makes it zero unless $y=x$; then P3 and P5 give the unique coefficient $n_d^2=1$. The left identity is proved in the same way, using cyclic symmetry with $\gamma_{x,y^{-1},d}$; the appropriate unique $d$ comes from P3 applied to $x^{-1}$. Step 1.1 proves that $\iota_J$ reverses products. Since $d=d^{-1}$ by P6, $\mu(t_xt_y)=\sum_d\gamma_{x,y,d}n_d$ is $\delta_{x,y^{-1}}$ by P2, P3 and P5. This symmetric permutation Gram matrix is invertible over $\mathbb Z$, proving every trace assertion.

P4 implies that each $I_i$ is a two-sided ideal. Its layer has exactly the stated basis since both ideals are spans of subsets of the $D$-basis. P8 and step 3.1 give the orthogonal ideal decomposition $J=\bigoplus_iJ^i$, with central identities $1_i=\sum_{d:a(d)=i}n_dt_d$. On the free layer $B_i$, identify $[D_w]$ with $t_w$ for $a(w)=i$ and give it the left regular $J^i_A$ action. Natural left and right $H$ multiplication are well defined on the layer.

Let $A_x$ be natural left multiplication by $D_x$ on $B_i$. The coefficient of $[D_y]$ in $A_xR_{t_{x'}}[D_w]$ is $\sum_uh_{x,u,y}\gamma_{w,x',u^{-1}}$; the coefficient in $R_{t_{x'}}A_x[D_w]$ is $\sum_uh_{x,w,u}\gamma_{u,x',y^{-1}}$. Here only indices of degree $i=a(w)=a(y)$ survive. P15′ gives equality. Thus $A_x$ commutes with every right regular $J^i_A$ multiplication and is left multiplication by its value on $1_i$. That value is $\sum_{z:a(z)=i}\sum_{d:a(d)=i}h_{x,d,z}n_dt_z$, the degree-$i$ component of the displayed $\phi(D_x)$. This proves compatibility of the left $H$ action with $\phi$.

Composition of natural left $H$ actions gives $L_{\phi(hh')}=L_{\phi(h)}L_{\phi(h')}$ on $\bigoplus_iJ_A^i$. Evaluating on its identity proves $\phi(hh')=\phi(h)\phi(h')$; evaluating the identity action proves $\phi(1_H)=1_J$. For the right $H$ action to commute with left $J$, apply P15′ with $(x,x',w,y)$ replaced by $(x^{-1},z^{-1},w^{-1},y^{-1})$ and replace the summation variable by its inverse. Using step 1.1 gives $\sum_u\gamma_{z,w,u^{-1}}h_{u,x,y}=\sum_uh_{w,x,u}\gamma_{z,u,y^{-1}}$, exactly the coefficient equality for $(t_z\cdot[D_w])D_x=t_z\cdot([D_w]D_x)$. Thus $B_i$ is the asserted bimodule. This argument requires no equality between $\phi$ and its opposite/adjoint version.

The bases, identities and multiplication equalities above are finite integral coefficient identities; they remain valid after every commutative base change. If $h\in\ker\phi_R$, compatibility says that $hI_i\subseteq I_{i+1}$ for all $i$. A product of $N+1$ such elements therefore kills $I_0=H_R$ and in particular its unit, proving the nilpotence bound. Over $K$, the algebra $H_K$ is a product of full matrix algebras by the given split generic hypothesis. A nilpotent two-sided ideal of such a product is zero: its intersection with any simple matrix factor is either zero or that factor, and a nonzero factor contains its identity and is not nilpotent. Thus $\phi_K$ is injective and, since both sides have dimension $|W|$, is an isomorphism.

Transport matrix units of $H_K$ through $\phi_K$. Their coordinates in the integral basis $t_w$ are rational functions of $v$, and their coordinate determinant is nonzero. Choose a rational value avoiding the finitely many zeros of their denominators and that determinant; such a value exists because a nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots and $\mathbb Q$ is infinite. Evaluating the coordinates preserves the finite matrix-unit and unit identities and retains their linear independence. They therefore give an isomorphism $J_{\mathbb Q}\cong\prod_E\operatorname{Mat}_{d_E}(\mathbb Q)$. After scalar extension back to $K$, this decomposition has the same primitive central blocks: in the center of a split matrix product every idempotent has only zero/one coordinates. Relabel its factors accordingly. This gives rational models $V_E$ for all generic labels. Finally the central orthogonal identities $1_i$ act on a simple module through exactly one component; its index is $\alpha_E$.

Work in the **split generic finite-Weyl setting**: $W$ is a finite Weyl group, $L:W\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ is a weight function, $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$, and $H=H_A(W,L)$ has the symmetric normalization $(T_s-v^{L(s)})(T_s+v^{-L(s)})=0$. Its KL basis is $C_w$. Write $K=\mathbb Q(v)$ and assume the generic algebra $H_K$ is split semisimple, as in the generic setup of [[def-canonical-basic-set-for-hecke-specialization]]. This hypothesis supplies the generic labels; this item asserts no new theorem on generic rational splitting. Let $\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ be the canonical symmetrizing trace.

The $A$-linear algebra involution $\dagger$ is $T_s\mapsto-T_s^{-1}$, and put $D_w=C_w^\dagger$. Define structure constants by $C_xC_y=\sum_z h_{x,y,z}C_z$; equivalently $D_xD_y=\sum_z h_{x,y,z}D_z$. Define

$$a(z)=\min\{n\ge0:v^n h_{x,y,z}\in\mathbb Z[v]\text{ for all }x,y\in W\},\qquad \gamma_{x,y,z}=[v^0](v^{a(z)}h_{x,y,z^{-1}}).$$

The integer $a(z)$ exists since $W$ is finite and all $h$ are Laurent polynomials invariant under bar. Let $\Delta(z)$ be the negative of the largest exponent in $\tau(C_z)$, and $n_z$ its nonzero coefficient. If $\tau(C_z)=0$, put $\Delta(z)=\infty$ and $n_z=0$. Let $\mathcal D=\{z:a(z)=\Delta(z)\}$. In particular $\Delta(1)=0$ and $n_1=1$; P3 below forces $a(1)=0$.

The following are **explicit hypotheses**, not assertions for every unequal weight. They are precisely the subset used in Geck section 5.2:

- P2: if $d\in\mathcal D$ and $\gamma_{x,y,d}\ne0$, then $x=y^{-1}$.
- P3: for every $y$ there is a unique $d\in\mathcal D$ with $\gamma_{y^{-1},y,d}\ne0$.
- P4: $h_{x,y,z}\ne0$ implies $a(z)\ge a(x)$ and $a(z)\ge a(y)$.
- P5: in P3, $\gamma_{y^{-1},y,d}=n_d=\pm1$.
- P6: every $d\in\mathcal D$ satisfies $d^2=1$.

Thus on a split product it is $\sum_Es_E\operatorname{Tr}_E$. Nondegeneracy forces every $s_E\ne0$, since otherwise an entire block is orthogonal to the algebra. Apply this to $J_{\mathbb Q}$ from [F1], and set $f_E=s_E^{-1}\in\mathbb Q^\times$. The same argument gives the generic Hecke Schur scalars in [F5].

Applying the matrix-coefficient functions gives $\sum_r\rho_G(b_r)_{ij}\rho_E(b_r^\vee)_{ab}=\delta_{G,E}f_E\delta_{i,b}\delta_{j,a}$. Summing the appropriate diagonal entries gives $\sum_r\chi_E(b_r)\chi_E(b_r^\vee)=f_E\dim V_E$. Let $z_E=\sum_w\chi_E^J(t_{w^{-1}})t_w\in J$. The coefficient identity in step 2.1 says that its action on $V_G$ is $\delta_{E,G}f_E\operatorname{id}$. Left multiplication by $z_E$ on the integral basis of $J$ has an integer matrix. The Cayley–Hamilton identity therefore shows that the rational number $f_E$ is an algebraic integer; a rational root of a monic integer polynomial is an integer, by clearing its reduced denominator in that polynomial. Hence $f_E\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$.

Put $a=\alpha_E$. The character of $E=K\otimes V_E$ satisfies $\chi_E(D_x)=\sum_{z,d:a(z)=a(d)=a}h_{x,d,z}n_d\chi_E^J(t_z)$ by [F1]. Each $v^ah_{x,d,z}$ is in $\mathbb Z[v]$ by the definition of $a(z)$. Taking its constant term gives $\sum_{z,d:a(z)=a(d)=a}\gamma_{x,d,z^{-1}}n_d\chi_E^J(t_z)=\chi_E^J(t_x)$, since $\sum_dn_dt_d$ is the identity of $J$ and all other support degrees act by zero. Thus $v^a\chi_E(D_x)\in\mathbb Z[v]$ and it is congruent to $\chi_E^J(t_x)$ modulo $v\mathbb Z[v]$.

To see positivity, use the rational positive definite form $\langle x,y\rangle=\mu(x\iota_J(y))$ on $J_{\mathbb Q}$: [F1] makes its basis $t_w$ orthonormal. Trace symmetry implies $\langle ax,y\rangle=\langle x,\iota_J(a)y\rangle$. A rational simple left ideal $U_E\subset J_{\mathbb Q}$ exists from its matrix decomposition and is invariant under both $a$ and $\iota_J(a)$; restriction of this positive form to $U_E$ is nondegenerate. In $J_S$ set $q_{ij}^E=f_E^{-1}\sum_w\rho_E(t_{w^{-1}})_{ji}t_w$. Step 2.1 gives $\rho_G(q_{ij}^E)=\delta_{E,G}e_{ij}$.
